title: Earth, Moon and Sun
scope: Use your school’s topic list to select the ideas you need. These are original practice questions with illustrative values and suggested self-marking guidance, not official Cambridge papers.

objectives.label: Explain day and night and distinguish rotation from orbital motion.
objectives.note: Relate Earth’s rotation to apparent solar motion and evaluate the scale and illumination limits of a globe-and-lamp model.

objectives.label: Explain opposite hemispheres’ seasons using tilt and sunlight geometry.
objectives.note: Use day length and energy per surface area; reject Earth–Sun distance alone as the cause of opposite seasons.

objectives.label: Explain lunar phases, synchronous rotation and the two lunar periods.
objectives.note: Separate the visible sunlit fraction from a shadow; distinguish the star-relative orbital period from the phase cycle.

objectives.label: Draw eclipse alignments and explain why eclipses do not occur every month.
objectives.note: Identify which body blocks light and how orbital tilt matters; distinguish apparent size from physical size and use safe indirect viewing only.

objectives.label: Explain tidal patterns and the limits of a two-bulge model.
objectives.note: Use differences in gravitational effects, distinguish spring and neap tides, and separate model patterns from real access-safety timetables.

cards.definition: Earth’s rotation changes which places face the Sun.
cards.explanation: Earth’s rotation changes which places face the Sun. A daily apparent motion across the sky does not mean the Sun orbits Earth once per day.
cards.example: A town passes into and out of the sunlit half as Earth rotates.
cards.confusion: A daily apparent motion across the sky does not mean the Sun orbits Earth once per day.

cards.definition: Earth’s axial tilt changes day length and sunlight angle over the year.
cards.explanation: Earth’s axial tilt changes day length and sunlight angle over the year. Distance from the Sun is not the main cause of opposite hemispheres’ seasons.
cards.example: When one hemisphere tilts towards the Sun it generally has longer days and higher solar altitude.

cards.definition: A phase is the fraction of the Moon’s sunlit half visible from Earth.
cards.explanation: A phase is the fraction of the Moon’s sunlit half visible from Earth. Ordinary phases are not Earth’s shadow falling on the Moon.
cards.example: A full Moon shows nearly all its sunlit half towards Earth.
cards.confusion: Ordinary phases are not Earth’s shadow falling on the Moon.

cards.answer: A phase is the fraction of the Moon’s sunlit half visible from Earth. Ordinary phases are not Earth’s shadow falling on the Moon.

cards.definition: An eclipse occurs when one body blocks light from reaching another body or observer.
cards.explanation: An eclipse occurs when one body blocks light from reaching another body or observer. There is not an eclipse at every new or full Moon because the Moon’s orbit is tilted.
cards.example: A solar eclipse can occur when the Moon passes between Earth and Sun in the right alignment.
cards.confusion: There is not an eclipse at every new or full Moon because the Moon’s orbit is tilted.

cards.explanation: Tides arise from differences in gravitational effects across Earth, with important local ocean responses. Actual high tide need not occur exactly when the Moon is overhead.
cards.example: The Sun and Moon together help produce spring and neap tidal patterns.
